strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel problem framing for mobile GUI agents: proactive task suggestion and personalized task execution, which addresses a real gap (existing benchmarks only test passive instruction-following with no user context).

Data collection effort is substantial and realistic: 95 users, one month of continuous real-life phone usage, 21,437 episodes across 506 apps, with rich contextual metadata (time, location, user profile, historical intents/actions) rather than crowdsourced or simulator-generated instructions.

Well-designed, non-trivial evaluation metrics (SR1/Sim1 for intent prediction, SR2/Sim2 for personalized execution with the different-user-type normalization) that attempt to capture nuanced notions of correctness and personalization rather than simple exact-match.

Broad and fair experimental coverage: multiple generalist MLLMs (GPT-4.1, Qwen-VL variants, DeepSeek-VL2, thinking model Qwen-QVQ-Max) and specialized GUI agents (Aguvis, CogAgent, UI-TARS, AutoDroid, AppAgent), plus a human study establishing a calibration point (30.3% human success vs 12.8% best model).

Extensive appendix ablations that strengthen the empirical claims: out-of-domain generalization (unseen users/apps/intents), contribution of each contextual signal, effect of probability-distribution outputs, a cheating/leakage check for the action-reference setup, and a user-rating validation of the Sim2 metric.

Fine-tuning experiments convincingly show that training on the collected data yields large, consistent gains over the base model and even surpasses stronger generalist baselines on some metrics, supporting the practical value of the dataset.
Reasonable ethics/privacy discussion and stated intent to open-source the data and collection app for reproducibility.
weaknesses: All 95 participants are from mainland China using Chinese apps; the paper acknowledges this but it substantially limits linguistic/UI generalizability of both the dataset and the derived findings.

Automatic metrics rely heavily on LLM judges (DeepSeek-V3 for SR1 and intent categorization) without reported human-agreement statistics for these specific automatic judgments, raising some concern about judge reliability/bias.

Sim2, the core personalization metric, is a fairly indirect heuristic (ratio of similarity to same user's most-similar action sequence vs. different-type users' most-similar sequence); its correlation with human perceived personalization is validated on only 200 episodes and 4 models, and the correlation, while positive, is not strong (e.g., GPT-4.1 has similar Sim2 to Qwen-2.5-VL-7B but different ratings).

Fine-tuning experiments are limited to a single 7B backbone (Qwen-2.5-VL-7B) with LoRA; no exploration of whether the benchmark's proactive/personalization signal transfers to larger or differently-architected models.

The personalized execution formulation assumes the agent is given a full reference action sequence of a similar past task, which is a strong and somewhat unrealistic assumption for a genuinely open personalization setting; the cheating check is only conducted for one model.

Because data collection and testing draw from the same 95 users (train/test split is temporal per user, not held-out users for the main experiments), the large gains from fine-tuning could partly reflect user-specific memorization rather than a generally transferable notion of personalization, though the appendix's user-unseen ablation partially mitigates this concern.

Given screenshots and accessibility trees are collected from real personal phone usage, exposure of latent PII in screenshots (beyond what automated privacy screening can catch) remains a residual risk that is only partially addressed.
The core contribution is a benchmark/dataset rather than a new modeling technique, so novelty is primarily in problem formulation and data collection rather than technical/methodological advances.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely underexplored problem formulation for mobile GUI agents: proactive task suggestion from contextual/historical signals and personalized task execution that respects individual user preferences, which is a meaningful departure from the purely instruction-following paradigm dominant in prior benchmarks.

Substantial, longitudinal, in-the-wild data collection effort (95 users, one month, 21,437 episodes, 506 apps) rather than relying on annotator-simulated or single-session data, which is more representative of real usage patterns and historical context than existing static benchmarks.

Extensive experimental coverage, including multiple generalist MLLMs and specialized GUI-control agents, plus a large set of ablations in the appendix (contribution of contextual info, screenshots vs. historical intents, probability-based intent prediction, out-of-domain generalization, connection between the two tracks, validity check of the personalization metric against human ratings).
Fine-tuning experiments show the collected data has practical utility, improving both proactive suggestion and personalization metrics over the base model.
Reasonable attention to ethics/privacy (data scrubbing, opt-in collection, anonymization) and an honest limitations section acknowledging single-region/single-language scope.
weaknesses: Data and users are drawn entirely from mainland China with Chinese apps and language; while acknowledged as a limitation, this substantially limits claims of generalizability of the benchmark and findings to other locales/app ecosystems.

The SR1 proactive-suggestion success metric relies on a single LLM (DeepSeek-V3) as binary judge of intent equivalence, with no reported human-agreement validation of this automatic judge, raising reliability concerns for the primary reported metric.

The personalization metric Sim2 (ratio of agent-trajectory similarity to same-user/-type reference vs. different-type reference) is a fairly indirect and somewhat opaque proxy for 'personalization'; its validation against human ratings (Table 13) is based on only 4 models and a coarse increasing trend rather than rigorous statistical correlation analysis.

All reported success rates are quite low across every evaluated model (best generalist SR1=12.8%, best specialized-agent SR2=38.5%, human SR1 only 30.3%), which could indicate the tasks are inherently under-specified or the ground-truth intents/actions are noisy/ambiguous (single free-text intent per instance, single 'golden' trajectory used for comparison despite acknowledged large variance across users), making it unclear whether low scores reflect model weakness or benchmark/label noise.

Out-of-domain generalization and human-rating validation experiments use very small subsets (as few as 99-126 episodes from 3-7 users/apps), limiting the statistical reliability of these secondary but important conclusions.

Only one base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) is used for the fine-tuning experiments, so claims about the practical value of the collected data for training are not demonstrated across architectures or model scales.

Users' behavior while explicitly using a data-collection app and being paid/monitored may not fully reflect naturalistic 'real life' usage, potentially introducing collection-induced biases not discussed.

Comparison table and related work, while reasonably thorough, could more directly engage with proactive/user-modeling agent literature outside the mobile GUI domain to better contextualize the technical novelty of the proposed formulation versus adapting existing proactive-assistant formulations to mobile.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and practically important benchmark direction: proactive task suggestion and personalized task execution for mobile LLM agents, which existing benchmarks (as summarized in Table 1) do not address.

Substantial, carefully engineered longitudinal data collection effort: 95 real users over one month, 21,437 episodes across 506 apps, with rich contextual metadata (time, location, user profile, historical intents/actions) collected via a custom-built accessibility-based app, rather than synthetic or simulator-collected data.

Reasonable, purpose-built metrics for both tracks (Sim1/SR1 combining embedding + Levenshtein similarity with LLM-judged binary success; Sim2/SR2 combining execution success with a personalization similarity measure relative to same-user/different-user action sequences), including a quantitative human-rating validation of Sim2 in the appendix (Table 13) showing meaningful correlation.

Reasonably broad and relevant evaluation covering generalist MLLMs (GPT-4.1, Qwen-VL variants, DeepSeek-VL2, Qwen-QVQ-Max) and specialized GUI-control agents (AutoDroid, AppAgent, Aguvis, CogAgent, UI-TARS), plus a human study establishing an upper-bound gap (30.3% vs best model 12.8% for proactive suggestion).

Extensive ablations and supplementary analyses in the appendix (out-of-domain generalization, contribution of screenshots/history/contextual fields, probability-distribution output setting, connection between the two tracks, cheating-sequence check), which substantially strengthen the empirical rigor and support the paper's claims.
Fine-tuning experiments show the collected data meaningfully improves both proactive suggestion and personalization metrics over the base model, supporting the claimed utility of the dataset.
Reasonably thorough ethics/privacy discussion (manual + LLM-assisted privacy screening, data usage agreements, broader impact discussion) given the sensitivity of collecting real personal usage data.
weaknesses: Data collected exclusively from 95 users in mainland China using predominantly Chinese apps; generalizability to other languages, cultures, and app ecosystems is unverified (acknowledged as a limitation but still a substantive constraint on claimed significance).

Sim2 (personalization metric) shows nearly identical values (~1.0) across almost all evaluated un-fine-tuned models in the main experiment, suggesting the metric may have limited discriminative power; only the fine-tuned models show a clear shift, validated only by a small-scale, indirect human study.

Ground-truth 'personalization' relies on assuming the single recorded human demonstration reflects a stable user preference, but many app tasks may have essentially unique/canonical solutions, so action-sequence variation may reflect UI noise rather than genuine preference; the paper's own action-similarity analysis (Figure 5) shows only modest differences between same-type and different-type users.

The proactive-suggestion task reduces an open-ended prediction problem to matching a single ground-truth intent via text-similarity/LLM-judge metrics; single best-effort predictions are penalized for plausible alternatives, and although Appendix A.6.5 explores a probability-distribution alternative, it is not used as the main evaluation, potentially overstating the human-model gap.

The human study for proactive suggestion (20 annotators, 400 episodes) is relatively small, and it is unclear whether human annotators had access to the same contextual signals/history as the models, which affects the validity of the human-vs-model comparison.
Fine-tuned model comparisons use only a single 7B backbone (Qwen-2.5-VL-7B) due to stated cost constraints, limiting confidence that improvements generalize across model scales/architectures.

Some evaluation choices are somewhat ad hoc (e.g., the LLM-judge criterion for 'same intent' in SR1, the 2.5x golden-steps failure threshold, reliance on DeepSeek-V3 for intent categorization and privacy screening) without reported inter-annotator agreement or judge-reliability checks.
Anonymized data/code links are not resolvable during review, limiting ability to verify reproducibility claims at this stage.
